```{python}
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/byuidatascience/data4missing/master/data-raw/flights_missing/flights_missing.json"
```

## QUESTION 1

1. __Convert values to missing__ Start with a fresh copy of the flights dataset by reading it in from the link provided above (as opposed to starting with the dataset you ended with in the last assignment). Identify data values that are problematic, non-sense or impossible and change them to be missing. In your report include one record example (one row) from your clean data, in the raw JSON format. Your example should display at least one missing value so that we can verify it was done correctly. (Note: JSON will convert NaN's to null). Describe your process for finding values that needed to be changed, and how you changed them.

I cleaned the data by first casting all the numeric columns to Int64 with pl.cast() with strict mode off, which takes any values that cannot be converted to numbers, such as '1500+', to null automatically. I then went through the rest of the numeric column data and took any negative numbers and made them null as well because negative delays should not be in this dataset. Last I took all the 'n/a'values for the months column and made them null as well to keep clean data

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
num_of_columns = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("num_of_")]
minutes_columns = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("minutes_delayed_")]

casted_columns = pl.col(num_of_columns).cast(pl.Int64, strict=False)


nulled_df = df.with_columns(
    pl.when(casted_columns < 0).then(None).otherwise(casted_columns).name.keep(),
    pl.when(pl.col(minutes_columns) < 0)
    .then(None)
    .otherwise(pl.col(minutes_columns))
    .name.keep(),
    pl.when(pl.col("month") == "n/a").then(None).otherwise(pl.col("month")).name.keep(),
)


example_row_json = json.dumps(nulled_df[0].to_dicts(), indent=1)

print(example_row_json)
```

## QUESTION 2

2. __Filling in missing data__ For all the "minutes_delayed" columns, fill in any missing values with the median of that column. For the "num_of" columns, fill in missing values with that column's mean.

_Nothing to write/report for this question_

```{python}

filled_df = nulled_df.with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col("month") == "January")
    .then(pl.col("year").fill_null(strategy="backward"))
    .otherwise(pl.col("year").fill_null(strategy="forward")),
    pl.col(minutes_columns).fill_null(pl.col(minutes_columns).median()),
    pl.col(num_of_columns).fill_null(strategy="mean"),
)

neg_df = filled_df.sort(pl.col("minutes_delayed_nas"), descending=False)
```

## QUESTION 3
 
3. __Display a histogram for num_of_delays_carrier and for minutes_delayed_nas (2 separate histograms in total). Comment on the shape of each one. Also report the mean of each of these columns now that missing values have been filled in.__

The carrier delays have an initial spike around 350 with a count of 62 followed by lesser and lesser counts as you go higher in the amount of delays—except for the 675-725 range where it spikes to 110. The mean value of the carrier delays column is 691, right within the range of the spike. For the NAS Minutes delayed we see a large spike from 0-25000 minutes delayed and then a dropoff further along the x axis, which I would expect as smaller delays are better for business. The mean for the minutes delayed by NAS is ~69,000 but it doesn't seem to disrupt the data in a meaningful way as the histogram's logarithmic shaped trend is followed.

```{python}
    ggplot(filled_df, aes("num_of_delays_carrier"))
    + geom_histogram(binwidth=50, boundary=0, fill="steel-blue", color="#000000")

    ggplot(filled_df, aes("minutes_delayed_nas"))
    + geom_histogram(binwidth=25000, boundary=0, fill="dark-red", color="#000000")
    + labs(x="Minutes Delayed By NAS", y="Count")
).show()
```
